blocks.text: Third, the Arabic verb سفع [safaʿa] saphaa, which means to scorch with a blast, seems to allude to the Hebrew צפע tsepha. Hence καύσωνες [kausōnes], scorching winds, are called سوافع [sawāfiʿ] ^{(1)}. For this is precisely the property of the basilisk: it scorches with its breath. Horapollo, book 1 [III, 185] of the Hieroglyphica, chapter 1: Προσφυσῆσαν ἑτέρῳ παντὶ ζώῳ (τοῦτο γένος,) δίχα καὶ τοῦ δακεῖν ἀναιρεῖ [Prosphysēsan heterō panti zōō (touto genos,) dicha kai tou dakein anairei]; This kind, if it has breathed upon any other animal, kills it even without a bite. And book 2, chapter 57: Τοὺς πλησιάζοντας τῷ ἑαυτοῦ φησήματι φονεύει [Tous plēsiazontas tō heautou phēsēmati phoneuei]; It kills those who approach with its breath. Aelian, Historia book 2, ch. 5: Θεασάμενος ὁ τῶν ὄφεων μήκιστος αὐτὸν, οὐκ εἰς ἀναβολὰς, ἀλλ᾽ ἤδη ἐκ τῆς τοῦ φυσήματος προσβολῆς αὐτός ἐστιν [Theasamenos ho tōn opheōn mēkistos auton, ouk eis anabolas, all᾽ ēdē ek tēs tou physēmatos prosbolēs autos estin] (read καυτὸς [kautos], or καυστός ἐστιν [kaustos estin]). A serpent, one of the very largest, on seeing it, is burnt up not after some delay but at once by the force of its breath. Pliny, book 8, chapter 21: It kills shrubs, not only those it touches but also those it breathes upon; it scorches grasses, it bursts rocks: such is the power of this evil creature. Solinus: It extinguishes grasses, kills trees, and corrupts even the very air. Therefore, just as the basilisk is called צפע tsepha, so سفع [safaʿa] saphaa, said of the wind, means to burn and to scorch, as the basilisk does, in whose breath there is a caustic power. The former, indeed, is written with Tsade, the latter with Sin. But among the Arabs the letters Sin and Sad or Sade are so interchangeable that they write countless words with either. Thus سلط [sallaṭa] or صلط [ṣallaṭa], he set in authority; اسلنطح [islanṭaḥa] or اصلنطح [iṣlanṭaḥa], it was broad; سوق [sūq] or صوق [ṣūq], street; [col. 402] سراط [sirāṭ] or صراط [ṣirāṭ], way, if written with Kesre, and long sword, if with Damma; سقاب [siqāb] or صقاب [ṣiqāb], a bloodied fillet, which Arab women wear when they have met with some grievous misfortune; سنط [sanṭ] or صنط [ṣanṭ], acacia; سعطر [saʿtar] or صعطر [ṣaʿtar], origanum; اسفنط [isfanṭ] or اصفنط [iṣfanṭ], a kind of drink made from grape juice seasoned with spices; سعوط [saʿūṭ] or صعوط [ṣaʿūṭ], an ἔῤῥινον [errhinon] for purging the head; مسمرط [musamraṭ] or مصمرط [muṣamraṭ], oblong of head, etc. ^{(2)}.

[III, 186] Fourth, even if there was no basilisk in Judaea, it could nevertheless have been known to the Jews through the Egyptians. For it was common in Egypt, and in Libya and Cyrenaica, which border on Egypt. Ammianus, book 22: Egypt also nourishes innumerable serpents, raging beyond all destructiveness: basilisks and amphisbaenas, etc. Pliny, book 8, chapter 21: The province of Cyrenaica produces it. Solinus: Behind Cyrene lie various barbarian nations, and an uncultivated wilderness, squalid and inaccessible, which breeds the basilisk. Aelian, book 3, chapter 31, calls Libya τὴν τῶν τοιούτων τροφὸν [tēn tōn toioutōn trophon], the land that nurtures such creatures. And Avicenna says it abounds ببلاد الترك ولوبية [bi-bilād al-Turk wa-Lūbiya] in the region of Turkey and Libya, not of Arorch and Nubia, as the translators have it. Thus the basilisk was very well known to the Egyptians, who in their language called it ΟΥΒΑΙ͂ΟΝ [ouBAION] (just as even today they call any serpent ʼΟΒΙῸΝ [obion]), and they placed a golden basilisk around the heads of the gods. And in their symbols they signified a sycophant by the basilisk, which kills by its breath alone, just as they signified eternity by the image of a basilisk hiding its tail beneath the rest of its body. See Horapollo, book 1, chapter 1, and book 2, chapter 57.
